topic: Labels or Instructions – Missing or Ambiguous Form Guidance
do: Provide clear and descriptive labels for all form fields, inputs, and interactive controls.
Use the <label> element with a for attribute linked to the input’s id for explicit labeling.
For form controls without visible labels (like search fields with only an icon), use aria-label or aria-labelledby to provide a programmatic label.
Provide inline instructions near the relevant form field (before or immediately after the input).
For groups of related controls (radio buttons, checkboxes), use <fieldset> and <legend> to provide group context.
Mark required fields using visible text (e.g., 'Required') and programmatic indication (required attribute or aria-required).
Provide examples of expected input formats (e.g., DD/MM/YYYY) close to the input field.
Ensure error messages identify the specific field and are programmatically linked via aria-describedby.
Ensure labels and instructions remain visible while entering data and do not disappear on focus.
Test with screen readers to confirm labels and instructions are announced in the correct order.
dont: Don’t leave form fields without labels or guidance on how to complete them.
Don’t rely solely on placeholder text as the label, since it disappears on typing and is not reliably announced.
Don’t rely only on the visual proximity of text to imply association; always create explicit programmatic relationships.
Don’t use vague labels such as 'Input' or 'Field' — be descriptive and specific.
Don’t use title attributes as the only labeling method; they are inconsistently supported by assistive technologies.
Don’t place instructions far from the related input in the DOM, breaking the logical reading sequence.
Don’t rely solely on color, styling, or symbols (like red borders or *) to indicate required fields or errors.
Don’t hide labels for visual minimalism without providing accessible alternatives.
Don’t provide error messages without associating them with their respective input fields programmatically.
edge_cases: Dynamically generated forms may inject inputs without labels, breaking accessibility.
Multi-step forms may lose context if instructions are not repeated for new sections.
Forms using ARIA-only labels may fail in older assistive technologies if no visible label is present.
Custom widgets (date pickers, sliders) may lack proper labels or instructions unless ARIA attributes are correctly applied.
Error messages placed visually near inputs may be missed by screen readers if not linked via aria-describedby.
Mobile responsive layouts may visually separate labels/instructions from their fields, confusing users.
Icon-only buttons or controls (e.g., search or close) must include aria-label to provide accessible names.
Single-page apps may re-render forms and break label associations if IDs are duplicated or mismatched.
Inputs rely on placeholder text instead of visible or persistent labels.
Form instructions or hints are not linked to their fields programmatically.
Required fields are indicated visually but not communicated to assistive technologies.
Error messages appear visually but are not announced or associated to the input field.
Automation tools often confirm labels but not instructional clarity or placement.
Complex form validation requirements not clearly communicated.
Multi-step form processes lacking clear navigation instructions.
Input format requirements not specified or unclear.
